section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of a Rotating Ray
section_1.content: Introduce the idea of a ray anchored at a point that rotates continuously. Explain that as the ray hits points in a 2D plane, it 'switches' its anchor point whenever it encounters a new point, maintaining a clockwise motion.
section_1.example: Imagine a flashlight beam rotating clockwise in a field of fireflies; every time the beam hits a new firefly, that firefly becomes the new pivot point for the beam.

section_2.title: Problem Definition: The Windmill Motion
section_2.content: Define the Windmill process: Given n points in a plane, a line rotates around a pivot point (one of the n points). When the line hits another point, that point becomes the new pivot. Visualize this as a 'geometric dance' where the line is the windmill blade.
section_2.example: Visualizing 5 points as stars in the sky. The 'blade' starts at Star A, sweeps until it hits Star B, then pivots to Star B to sweep for Star C.

section_3.title: Core Mechanism: Angles and Pivot Switching
section_3.content: Explain the logic of switching: The line rotates until it is collinear with two points. The 'next' pivot is the point that preserves the clockwise rotational direction. This is a greedy algorithm approach.
section_3.example: An animation showing a clock hand. When it hits a point, the hand 'snaps' its center to that point and continues the sweep, ensuring the line never rotates counter-clockwise.

section_4.title: Theorem & Result: The Periodicity
section_4.content: Present the key knowledge point: The windmill process is periodic. For n points, the line will return to its original state after a finite number of rotations. Emphasize that the total number of turns is related to the permutation of points.
section_4.example: A diagram showing the line completing a full 180-degree sweep cycle, demonstrating that the 'blade' effectively explores all possible line orientations defined by the set of points.

section_5.title: Application and Conclusion
section_5.content: Briefly mention that this process is used in computer science for calculating convex hulls and point-set triangulation. Summarize how geometry turns into predictable patterns.
section_5.example: A 'Robot Vacuum' analogy: The vacuum (windmill blade) scans the room by pivoting on furniture legs to map the entire floor efficiently.

        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        self.play(FadeIn(anchor), Create(ray))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFF00")
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===

        self.play(FadeIn(point))
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFF00")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
